title: Weeks of supply: formula, example, and how planners use it
summary: Weeks of supply is stock on hand divided by forecast weekly demand. See the formula, a worked example, and why 6.0 weeks on past sales can mean 3.6 ahead.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 23 November 2026.


Weeks of supply is the number of weeks your current stock will last at the expected rate of sale. You calculate it by dividing inventory on hand by average weekly demand, so 2,400 units against a demand of 400 units a week is 6.0 weeks of supply.


The calculation takes ten seconds, and the choice of "average weekly demand" decides whether the answer is useful. Divide by the last four weeks of sales and you describe the past. Divide by the forecast and you describe the weeks the stock actually has to cover, which is the question a planner is asking.


This guide covers the weeks of supply formula on one retailer, the gap between the trailing and forward versions, how to set a target, and how the reading changes between a store, a distribution center (DC), and the end of a season. If you would rather see the forward figure on your own range, you can[walk through your stock cover with our team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- Weeks of supply = inventory on hand ÷ average weekly demand. With 2,400 units and 400 units sold a week, the result is 6.0 weeks.
- The same 2,400 units cover only 3.6 weeks when the divisor is a rising pre-peak forecast (500, 600, 750, then 900 units a week) in place of past sales.
- US retailers held 1.35 months of sales in stock in September 2026, about 5.9 weeks (US Census Bureau). Clothing stores held 2.01 months and food and beverage stores 0.82.
- A workable target is lead time plus review period plus safety buffer: a 5-week lead time, a weekly review, and 2 weeks of buffer give 8 weeks for stock on hand and on order.
- Days of inventory on hand (DIO) looks back at cost of goods sold. Weeks of supply looks forward at demand, and in the worked example the two readings sit 2.4 weeks apart just before a peak.


## What is weeks of supply?


Weeks of supply (WOS) is an inventory coverage metric that expresses stock as time. It divides the inventory you hold by the weekly demand you expect, and the result is the number of weeks that stock will last if nothing else arrives. Retail planners use it to decide when to reorder, where to send stock, and how much is too much.


You will also hear weeks of cover, weeks of stock, and forward cover. Teams use these names loosely, and the real difference between two reports is nearly always the divisor. A trailing calculation uses recent sales, and a forward calculation uses the forecast.


The retail management course published by Lumen Learning describes both. It defines weeks of supply as the inventory position for a period divided by average sales, and forward weeks of supply as the number of weeks of planned sales, from next week onward, that current inventory represents. The course also warns that a high-sales period such as Easter makes the trailing figure look artificially low.


Expressing stock as time is what makes the metric practical. A buyer cannot judge 2,400 candles and 310 sofas on the same scale in units or in euros. In weeks, both can be compared with the lead time needed to get more.


## The weeks of supply formula, with a worked example


**Weeks of supply = inventory on hand ÷ average weekly demand**


Inventory on hand is the sellable stock for the perimeter you are measuring, in units. Average weekly demand is either an average of recent weekly sales (trailing) or the forecast for the coming weeks (forward). Both sides must cover the same products and the same locations.


Take a home goods retailer with 28 stores and one DC, and its best-selling large scented candle (an illustrative example with our own arithmetic, reused in every section).


1. Stock on hand in early October: 2,400 units, of which 1,400 are in stores and 1,000 at the DC.
2. Sales over the last four weeks: 380, 390, 410, and 420 units, an average of 400 a week.
3. Trailing weeks of supply: 2,400 ÷ 400 = 6.0 weeks.


### Forward weeks of supply


The forward version replaces past sales with the forecast and counts how many future weeks the stock covers. The candle sells mostly in the last quarter, and the forecast for the next five weeks is 500, 600, 750, 900, and 1,000 units.


1. Week 1 takes 500 units and leaves 1,900.
2. Week 2 takes 600 and leaves 1,300.
3. Week 3 takes 750 and leaves 550.
4. Week 4 needs 900, so the remaining 550 units cover 0.6 of that week.


Forward weeks of supply is 3.6 weeks. Some teams divide stock by the average forecast over a fixed horizon, which is quicker in a spreadsheet. Counting week by week is more accurate when demand is rising or falling, because it uses each week's own forecast.


Here is how that plays out for Ines, the retailer's replenishment planner (an illustrative case). Her weekly report showed 6.0 weeks of supply on the candle against a supplier lead time of 5 weeks, so the product was not flagged. The forward calculation showed 3.6 weeks, which meant an order placed that day would land after the shelf was empty.


Demand over the five weeks of lead time adds up to 3,750 units against 2,400 in stock. The gap before the next delivery was 1,350 units, in the two best weeks of the year. One mistake we repeatedly see is a weeks of supply report built on the trailing four weeks and reviewed in the first week of a peak, when the past is the worst available guide to the next month.


### Units, value, and on-order stock


At product level, calculate weeks of supply in units. Above product level, units stop making sense, so use value at cost on both sides: inventory at cost divided by forecast cost of goods sold (COGS) per week. The retailer's home textiles category holds €540k of stock at cost against forecast COGS of €780k over the next 13 weeks, or €60k a week, which gives 9.0 weeks.


Decide once whether on-order stock is included, and label the figure. Stock on hand answers "when do I run out if nothing arrives?". Stock on hand plus confirmed orders answers "is enough already coming?", and it is the version to compare with a reorder target.


## Weeks of supply vs days of inventory on hand


The two metrics look like the same number in different units, and on paper they convert. Weeks of supply equals DIO divided by 7, and it also equals 52 divided by inventory turnover. A category that turns four times a year holds about 91 days of inventory, or 13 weeks.


That conversion only holds when both use the same divisor.[Days of inventory on hand](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/days-of-inventory-on-hand) is a finance measure: average or closing inventory at cost, divided by the COGS already booked over a past period. It tells a CFO how much cash sat in stock last quarter. Weeks of supply, in its forward form, divides today's stock by the demand that has not happened yet.

For the candle, a backward measure says 6.0 weeks (42 days) and the forward one says 3.6. Neither is wrong, and they answer different questions. In a flat week of a flat category the two will agree closely, and the weeks before a peak or after a launch are where they split.


## What is a good weeks of supply?


There is no universal number, and any figure quoted without a lead time attached should be treated with caution. The useful comparison is between the cover you have and the time you need to get more.


### Build the target from lead time


A workable target for stock on hand plus on order is the sum of three durations: supplier lead time, the review period between two ordering decisions, and a safety buffer expressed in weeks. For the candle, that is 5 weeks of lead time, a weekly review, and 2 weeks of buffer, or 8 weeks.


The order then follows from the forecast. Demand over the next eight weeks is forecast at 6,050 units (500, 600, 750, 900, 1,000, 1,000, 800, and 500). Ines holds 2,400 with nothing on order, so the order that restores the target is 3,650 units.


The buffer is where service level enters. Two weeks is a placeholder here, and the right figure depends on how variable demand and lead time are for that product. Our guide to[safety stock optimization](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/safety-stock-optimization) covers how to size it, and the result converts into weeks by dividing by forecast weekly demand.


### What public data shows


The US Census Bureau publishes a monthly inventories to sales ratio by kind of retail business: the value of stock at month end divided by that month's sales. It is a backward-looking, sector-wide cousin of weeks of supply, and it shows how far normal cover differs between sectors.


Kind of business (US)Inventories to sales ratio, months (September 2026)Approximate weeks (our arithmetic)All retailers1.355.9Clothing and clothing accessory stores2.018.7Furniture, home furnishings, electronics, and appliance stores1.767.6Food and beverage stores0.823.6


The last column multiplies the ratio by 52 and divides by 12. Read it as an order of magnitude: the ratio compares stock valued at cost with sales at retail prices, so cover measured in units is longer than these figures suggest. Clothing stores still carry about two and a half times the cover of food stores, which is why a single target for a multi-category retailer makes little sense.


Sector figures are a sanity check and nothing more. For finance-side comparisons, our article on[what a good DIO looks like by retail sub-sector](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/good-dio-for-retail) goes further. For planning, compare each product's weeks of supply with its own target and with its own history.


## How planners read weeks of supply in stores and at the DC


A network figure is the sum of positions that do different jobs. The candle's 2,400 units are 1,400 on shelves and 1,000 in reserve, and the two parts should be read separately.


### Store level


Stores are replenished often, so they need little cover: enough for the days between two deliveries, plus a display minimum and a small buffer. The 28 stores hold 1,400 candles, which covers the first two weeks of forecast (500 and 600 units) and 0.4 of the third, or 2.4 weeks forward. For a product delivered twice a week, that is comfortable.


The average hides the spread between stores. Tomás, the allocation manager, looked at one throw blanket in two stores that each held 120 units (an illustrative case). The city-center store was forecast to sell 40 a week and the retail park store 10, so the same 120 units meant 3.0 weeks in one and 12.0 in the other.


With a store target of 4 weeks, the first store was 40 units short and the second carried 80 units more than it needed. Tomás sent the DC's next delivery to the city-center store only and scheduled no replenishment for the retail park until its cover fell below target. Our article on[rebalancing stock between stores](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/rebalancing-allocation-stores) covers when a transfer is worth its cost.


### DC and network level


The DC's job is to cover supplier lead time for the whole network. Its 1,000 candles should be read against network demand, since every store draws on them. After the stores' own 2.4 weeks, the reserve adds just over one more week at peak rates.


Add in-transit and on-order stock and you get the network position, the number to compare with the 8-week target. Across Metreecs' work with multi-store retailers, the network total often looks healthy while the stock sits in the wrong place: reserve held back at the DC during the weeks when stores sell fastest, or pushed out to stores that will not sell it. Reading weeks of supply at each level shows which of the two is happening.


## Weeks of supply across a season


For seasonal products, the target moves through the season and the comparison changes at the end.


Before the season, cover is deliberately high because stock arrives ahead of the sales it supports. A trailing calculation in those weeks produces alarming numbers, since stock is divided by pre-season sales. The forward version, divided by the forecast for the opening weeks, shows whether the build-up matches the plan.


Just after a peak the distortion reverses. The trailing average still contains the peak weeks, so weeks of supply looks low and invites a reorder the coming weeks will not absorb. This is the Easter effect described in the Lumen course, and it applies equally to the first weeks of January.


At the end of the season, compare weeks of supply with the weeks left to sell. Priya manages outdoor cushions for the same retailer (an illustrative case). With five weeks left in the season, she held 1,800 units against a forecast of 250, 220, 200, 180, and 150 units, or 1,000 in total.


Her weeks of supply at the average forecast rate was 9.0 against five weeks remaining. That put 800 units, 44% of the stock, on course to be left over at full price. Knowing it five weeks early gave her time to act store by store, starting with the highest cover, before a chain-wide markdown became the only option.


## Where weeks of supply misleads


Four situations produce a figure that looks precise and points the wrong way. Each has a structural cause, and each can be checked.


### Stockouts shrink the divisor


A product that was out of stock sells nothing, and a trailing average counts those weeks as low demand. Suppose a product sold 100 units a week for two weeks, then sat empty for two. Its four-week average is 50, so a 600-unit delivery shows 12 weeks of supply when the true figure is 6. Exclude out-of-stock weeks from the average, or use a forecast built on unconstrained demand.


### Averages hide the variant mix


The retailer's bed linen range holds 1,600 units against a forecast of 200 a week, or 8.0 weeks. The double size accounts for 75 of those 200 units and has 150 in stock, which is 2.0 weeks. The other sizes hold 1,450 units for 125 a week, or 11.6 weeks.


The category looks balanced, while one size is about to run out and the rest are overstocked. The planners we work with often underestimate how much of a healthy category figure comes from variants that barely sell. Weeks of supply only supports a decision at the level where the decision is taken, which for replenishment is the variant and the location.


### Slow and intermittent sellers


When a product sells one unit every few weeks, the divisor is close to zero and the result swings between 20 weeks and infinity. The metric carries little information for these items. A minimum presentation quantity per store and a count of weeks since the last sale are more useful.


### The forecast carries its own error


Forward weeks of supply is only as good as the forecast under it. If demand for the candle comes in 20% above forecast, 3.6 weeks becomes about 3.2. This is a reason to keep the safety buffer in the target, and to refresh the calculation every week during a peak.


All four limits come back to the divisor. A weekly demand figure per product and per location, corrected for stockouts and updated as sales arrive, is what turns the ratio into something a planner can order against. ## FAQ


### How do I calculate weeks of supply?


Divide inventory on hand by average weekly demand, both measured on the same products and locations. Use units for a single product and value at cost for a category. For a forward-looking figure, subtract each coming week's forecast from stock until it runs out and count the weeks.


### What is the difference between weeks of supply and days of inventory on hand?


Days of inventory on hand divides inventory at cost by the COGS of a past period, and finance teams use it to track cash tied up in stock. Weeks of supply is a planning measure, usually divided by forecast demand. They convert (weeks = days ÷ 7) only when demand is stable.


### Is weeks of supply the same as weeks of cover?


In most companies, yes. Both divide stock by a weekly rate of sale. Before comparing two reports, check whether the rate is past sales or a forecast, how many weeks it averages, and whether on-order stock is included.


### Should on-order stock be included in weeks of supply?


It depends on the question. Leave it out to see when the shelf empties if nothing arrives. Include confirmed orders when you compare cover with a reorder target, and say on the report which version is shown.


### How many weeks of supply should a retailer hold?


Enough to cover supplier lead time, the time between two ordering decisions, and a safety buffer for demand and delivery variability. That can mean 2 weeks in a store replenished twice a week and 12 or more for an imported product. A single company-wide target is rarely right for any category.


### Why does my weeks of supply jump from week to week?


A trailing figure moves with last week's sales, so a promotion, a stockout, or a holiday shifts it without any change in stock. Lengthening the averaging window smooths it and makes it slower to react. A forecast-based figure is steadier because the forecast already accounts for those events.


## Conclusion


Weeks of supply turns stock into time, which lets you compare it directly with lead times and with the weeks left in a season. Calculate it forward on the forecast, set the target from lead time, review period, and buffer, and read it by variant and location so an average cannot hide a shortage.
